Yo, Rider's Republic is an absolute banger. If you’re into chaotic energy, adrenaline rushes, and flexing your drip while shredding mountains, this game is your playground.
First off, the map is massive—like, you blink and suddenly you’re in Bryce Canyon doing backflips on a snowmobile. The devs really said “why not all the national parks?” and we’re here for it. The terrain is chef’s kiss: snow, dirt, cliffs, forests—every inch is begging to be explored or absolutely yeeted off.
Gameplay? Smooth like butter. You can switch between biking, skiing, snowboarding, wingsuiting, and even rocket wings (yes, rocket wings, it’s giving Tony Stark energy). Controls are tight, physics are wild but fair, and the tricks system makes you feel like a pro even if you’re just button mashing.
Multiplayer is where it slaps hardest. Mass races are pure chaos— players barreling down a mountain like caffeinated squirrels. It’s hilarious, it’s sweaty, it’s peak dopamine. And the social hub? It’s like a skatepark met TikTok and had a baby. You can vibe, emote, squad up, or just flex your gear.
Customization is 🔥 too. You wanna ride a BMX in a giraffe onesie? Go off, king. The gear drops are frequent and the fits are drippy. Ubisoft really understood the assignment.
Rider's Republic is the ultimate “touch grass but make it digital” experience. It’s chaotic, it’s gorgeous, it’s endlessly replayable. If you’re not playing it, wyd?
10/10 would crash into a tree again. 🌲💥

It's pretty awesome. I mainly got this game for the Skateboarding and the BMX. At first when I tried the skateboarding, I wanted to throw my computer through the window. But.....after about an hour of getting used to the skateboarding controls it became pretty good. Its the best skateboarding in a game I've found in a while. The reasons: Good graphics, good animations, It feels complete, and while the physics may not be the most realistic, its fun. Now that I've mastered the controls this is my favorite skateboarding game on PC. It looks good enough to have a realistic tone, unlike Tony hawk games, yet its not so difficult that it takes you a year to do a good run, like session. Its balanced. 

The BMX gameplay is really good, and it reminds me of the old Matt Hoffman's pro bmx, and Dave Mirra games on PS1/PS2. The Bicycling in this game is easier to grasp than the skateboarding, but the animations and how to feels to ride the bikes is very satisfying. 

The mountain biking looks good, feels good, and if you know the right spots on the map you can have a really good downhill run.  

Seeing how I only bought this game for the Skateboarding and Bicycles I won't touch on the rest of it, but there is so much to do here from skiing to flying with a jetpack. It all looks and feels good. This is one of the only games I have bought in recent years and didn't regret it. I got the skate edition on sale for $6, and it was the best $6 I've ever spent. I think its worth it at full price probably if you plan to utilize the game for its entirety and not just for one or two aspects of it.

This game is pretty debatable. I'd only recommend picking it up if it's on a big sale. It just doesn't feel like it deserves full price since there's nothing super gripping about it, and who knows how soon Ubisoft will shut down the servers. Plus, it wouldn't be Ubisoft if they didn't call an edition "Complete Edition" when it doesn't even include all the content.

The good stuff about the game is that it can definitely be fun. There are a bunch of activities, and the soundtrack is surprisingly good. Fast travel between races is super convenient, which helps to zip through career mode. Riders Republic is beginner-friendly, and coming in first isn't even necessary. But some tracks can really surprise, or even annoy. That's because it's tough to nail all the requirements for a perfect run (though, again, it's totally not required!).

The handling physics are arcade-style. That means the character and vehicle don't have a lot of inertia, allowing for tricks that are impossible in real life. It's fun when an extreme sports game forgives mistakes, but sometimes it feels like it needs a little more hardcore action. For example, skateboarding here is way too arcadey; smoother transitions between tricks, like in the Tony Hawk series, would be a welcome addition. Skiing is okay, but it's simplified compared to its predecessor, Steep, which had more realistic and hardcore physics. Bike handling is decent. Pedaling and doing tricks are both fun, and that's something that really clicked with me.

Among the debatable aspects, there's the weird map where roads bend unnaturally, and the different areas just don't make sense geographically. However, this kind of layout does allow for crazy tracks, so that decision is understandable. A surprising miss for a game where cool tricks and showing them off are part of the fun is the lack of an instant replay after finishing a race, and no way to record or rewatch a past race.

Probably the biggest downside of the game is its poor adaptation for keyboard controls. It was impossible to enjoy with such clunky controls, so a switch to a gamepad was necessary. The game feels totally different then, allowing for precise movement control, but at the same time, it demands pretty exact control with the left stick and triggers. After about an hour and a half of playing, hands were super tired, but there wasn't any discomfort.

This review is based on only 90 minutes of gameplay. Perhaps opinions will change later, but for now, getting the game on sale has been satisfying - it turned out better than expected.

Riders Republic is a gateway introduction to extreme sports set in exciting environments. It's a great game that can be picked up or put down with a minimal learning curve while still providing some adrenaline-packed moments of excitement. Although the racing may seem hypercompetitive, the atmosphere is very casual, silly, and customizable. The game has little linearity and is primarily a giant creative sandbox environment to try different sports in racing, tricks, and scenic exploration. I found the snow sports most enjoyable. Just try not to crash into a tree or a rock, and you'll be bound to have a great time.

Riders Republic is an incredibly underrated racing game that turns America's most famous and scenic national parks into extreme sports playgrounds. Riders allows the player to seamlessly change between snowboarding, skiing, paragliding, jetpacking, mountain biking, and so much more through the press of a button at any time. The world is populated with players and ghosts to keep it feeling truly alive, and the parks are interconnected without loading screens so that you can snowboard down the mountains of Mammoth Cave National Park, jump off that big ramp, and switch to your mountain bike as you land in the valleys of Zion. 

The game contains all kinds of events to play such as races, tricks battles, multi-sport races where the sport changes mid-race, and 'mass races' which feature up to 64 players in a single race. Mass races are still populated with many players years after release thanks to cross-play and the game is consistently updated to be fresh with a weekly rotation of different mass races, and new sports such as BMX and Skateboarding being added with their own events to play in seasonal updates. The game also features real-world brands such as Vans, Prada, and Red Bull (to name a few) that your Rider can be adorned with.

Riders Republic is an exhilarating and expansive extreme sports game that combines the thrill of downhill racing with the freedom of an open-world environment. Developed by Ubisoft Annecy, this title offers players the opportunity to engage in a variety of sports, including mountain biking, skiing, snowboarding, wingsuit flying, and more, all within a massive, seamlessly connected map that merges several iconic U.S. national parks. The game aims to capture the essence of extreme sports culture while providing an accessible and entertaining experience for both casual players and enthusiasts.

One of the standout features of Riders Republic is its vast and diverse open world. The game seamlessly integrates seven distinct national parks—Bryce Canyon, Yosemite Valley, Sequoia Park, Zion, Canyonlands, Mammoth Mountain, and Grand Teton—into a single, expansive map. This design allows players to traverse varied terrains, from snow-capped mountains to arid deserts, all in one continuous journey. The attention to detail in recreating these landscapes is commendable, offering a visually stunning backdrop for the high-octane action that unfolds.

The gameplay is designed to be accessible yet challenging. Players can choose from a range of disciplines, each with its own set of mechanics and nuances. The controls are intuitive, allowing newcomers to jump in and enjoy the game without a steep learning curve. However, for those seeking a more in-depth experience, the game offers opportunities to master tricks, refine techniques, and compete in various events. The inclusion of a rewind feature further enhances the accessibility, enabling players to correct mistakes without significant penalties.

Multiplayer modes are a significant draw in Riders Republic. The Mass Races, which can accommodate up to 64 players, are chaotic and exhilarating, offering a unique blend of competition and camaraderie. These races are scheduled periodically, and while the anticipation adds to the excitement, some players have expressed a desire for more flexibility in matchmaking. Additionally, the Tricks Battle Arena mode introduces a team-based competitive element, where players perform tricks to control specific areas and score points. These multiplayer modes add depth and replayability to the game, fostering a vibrant online community.

While the game excels in many areas, it is not without its shortcomings. Some players have noted that the world, despite its size and beauty, can feel empty at times. The vast distances between events can lead to moments of monotony, and the lack of engaging activities outside of races and challenges may detract from the overall experience. Additionally, the game's reliance on microtransactions for cosmetic items has been a point of contention. While these purchases do not affect gameplay, the presence of premium currency and rotating store items can create a sense of urgency and pressure to spend real money.

In conclusion, Riders Republic is a bold and ambitious title that successfully captures the excitement and freedom of extreme sports. Its expansive world, diverse gameplay options, and engaging multiplayer modes provide a compelling experience for players seeking adventure and adrenaline. While it may not be perfect, the game's strengths far outweigh its weaknesses, making it a worthwhile addition to the library of any action sports enthusiast. Whether you're racing down mountains, performing aerial stunts, or exploring the great outdoors, Riders Republic offers an exhilarating journey that is both thrilling and rewarding.

I was really excited for this game to hit steam because this is absolutely my kind of game. I love bike sports and other non-engine sports, especially when they're open world and open ended. I got it instantly upon release and I was only able to get a half an hour in before deciding to refund it.

There is explicitly one reason that convinced me to refund it and it's the absolutely unbearable controls. It feels like the game won't let you play it, or that your bike is sifting through a thick layer of viscous goo. It expects you to hold the left stick full in either direction for turns, which will cause it to slowly accelerate into turning until it viscerally snaps into a full turn. If you try and compensate for that by turning the other way, you have to hope there's enough time for the turn acceleration to catch up otherwise you're SOL. Outside of turning you just have very little control over any of the sports and everything feels so forced and clunky.

You have the option to 'drift' by holding left trigger to increase your turn speed, which it does, so much so that it's incredibly difficult to control. It does count as a form of breaking still, though, so it will slow you down significantly. Your options are either don't turn enough or turn far too much and lose a lot of speed in the process. I'd say tweak the games control settings but there really aren't any, not any that matter anyway.

If you're coming to this game as a more casual racing game player you're probably more likely to enjoy it, but coming to this after playing many racing games (and REALLY loving Descenders), this game just takes so much control away from the player that it's not remotely fun or satisfying for me. I love any genre of racing game from arcade to full on sim but these are easily the worst controls I've ever experienced. It feels like I'm fighting someone who's actively trying to counter my every input, or multiply it, like I had given a little sibling a second controller and they're trying their best to make the game as unplayable as possible.

Feel free to try it on your own and form your own opinion, refunding is always an option, I seem to be in the minority.

Honestly, this game is a major letdown. I had high hopes going in, especially as a fan of Steep, but Riders Republic just feels like Ubisoft tried to cram every extreme sport possible into one package without actually thinking about how it all fits together.

The graphics? Buggy. Glitches everywhere. Textures don’t load, characters randomly freak out, and it just feels unfinished—like a beta that got released too early. Compared to Steep, which felt focused and visually immersive, this is a chaotic mess.

Sure, it has tons of tricks and sports, but it all feels forced. The core gameplay loop is mostly just rushing downhill as fast as possible, and while that can be fun for a bit, it gets repetitive real quick. The "variety" in the map? Just different biomes—snow, dirt, desert—same gameplay, different skin. No real depth. It’s not Downhill Domination, no matter how much it tries to look cool.

Worst of all? The DLC situation. It’s brutal. Every day it feels like there’s a new paid feature, and half the time it’s stuff that should’ve been in the base game. If you didn’t buy the Ultimate Edition, good luck. Grinding for gear or access is a chore, and it honestly starts to feel more like a money pit than a game.

This isn't about being picky—it’s about a game that tried to do everything and ended up doing nothing really well. If you're not buying the full-priced ultimate version, save yourself the frustration. Not recommended.

I had multiple paragraphs written about all the issues I have with Rider's Republic, why I have low expectations for AAA games in general and how this one in particular still managed to let me down, and so on.

But nobody wants to read another wall of text from an overtired idiot as he nitpicks a bunch of tiny annoyances and the industry at large. I'll stick to the big one. Well, the biggest big one.

The biggest issue with Rider's Republic is the camera and lack of camera adjustment. The first of the third-person cameras moves around a bit but spends most of its time too close and too low directly behind your character's back, making it difficult or impossible to see directly in front of you. The second one is thankfully zoomed out a bit, but it's even lower and off to the side so now it's hard to judge exactly where you're facing beyond having just a general idea. Some games do the second "off-to-the-side" camera angle pretty well but this isn't one of them. I'm sure it's great for low-speed flatland tricks on a skateboard but not for anything else. Riders Republic Review: A Mixed Bag of Thrills and Frustrations

After spending about five hours with Riders Republic, I regret buying it. Developed by Ubisoft, the game promises thrilling, multi-sport action, but ultimately stumbles in key areas that make it a frustrating experience. Here’s a breakdown of my thoughts:

The Good
	•	Artwork and Presentation: The vibrant visual style is one of the game’s strongest points. The environments are diverse and well-designed, which makes exploring the massive map somewhat enjoyable.
	•	Adrenaline-Fueled Races: The races are a definite highlight. While stacking (colliding with other players or objects) can be frustrating, the chaotic nature of the gameplay keeps you on edge. It’s annoying to fall behind after a crash, but the game does a decent job of keeping you in the action, which is impressive given the fast-paced and competitive nature of the events.

The Bad
	•	Always-Online Requirement: Even in single-player mode, Riders Republic requires a constant internet connection. This is a major downside, especially given Ubisoft’s history of shutting down servers for older games. The idea that this game could become unplayable in the future is a huge red flag.
	•	Clunky Control Scheme: If you’re expecting smooth and intuitive controls like in the Skate series (Skate 3), prepare for disappointment. The controls are arcade-like, closer to Tony Hawk, but they feel poorly implemented and unresponsive, which undermines the gameplay.
	•	Bland and Over-the-Top Storyline: The storyline is exaggerated and tries way too hard to be quirky and energetic. It ends up feeling cringeworthy and unnecessary.
	•	DLC Disappointments: I purchased all the DLCs, but many features, like the longboard, remain locked or unusable. The skate DLC is particularly bad, feeling like a lazy, uninspired addition that adds no real value to the game.
	•	Price: Both the base game and the DLC are expensive, and for a game with so many flaws, it’s hard to justify the high cost.

The Verdict

While Riders Republic has its moments, particularly with the adrenaline-filled races, it struggles to deliver a consistently enjoyable experience. The clunky controls, always-online requirement, and overpriced content drag it down. If Ubisoft had refined the gameplay and offered more accessible features, this could’ve been a standout title. Instead, it’s a game that will only appeal to a niche audience.

Unless you’re a die-hard fan of arcade sports games, I recommend holding off—especially at full price.

[h1] 🚴‍♂️ Riders Republic – A Chaotic Extreme Sports Playground That Falls Flat [/h1]

[h2] Review Date: [/h2]
March 15, 2025

[h2] Reviewer Name: [/h2]
Schqrk Reviews

[h2] ⭐ Overall Rating: [/h2]
5/10

[h2] Completion: [/h2]
Didn't finish – lost interest before completing most events.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Introduction [/h2]
Riders Republic presents itself as a spiritual successor to games like Steep, but with a focus on high-energy, arcade-style gameplay rather than realistic physics. The game drops you into a massive open world inspired by real-life national parks, giving you the freedom to explore, compete in extreme sports events, and participate in large-scale multiplayer races.

At first glance, the game seems like a dream for fans of extreme sports, but beneath its flashy presentation, I found it to be repetitive, clunky, and lacking depth. While there are moments of fun—especially in multiplayer races—the overall experience suffers from unpolished mechanics, frustrating controls, and an over-the-top attempt at being "cool" that feels forced.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Graphics and Visuals [/h2]

[✔️] 🌄 The game’s world is massive and visually diverse, combining several famous national parks into one open playground. The environments look great from a distance, with towering mountains, lush forests, and vast deserts providing plenty of variety.

[✔️] ☀️ Dynamic weather effects, such as snowstorms and changing daylight cycles, add to the immersion. Seeing the sun set over the mountains or racing through thick fog does make for some cool moments.

[❌] 🎭 While the game looks good at times, up close, the textures are often low-resolution, and there’s noticeable pop-in when moving at high speeds. Some areas lack the level of detail expected from a modern open-world game.

[❌] 🤖 Character models and animations feel stiff, making tricks and movements look awkward rather than smooth. The exaggerated physics don’t help, often making crashes and landings look unnatural.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Gameplay and Mechanics [/h2]

[✔️] 🚴 The variety of extreme sports is a definite highlight. You can seamlessly switch between biking, skiing, snowboarding, and even wingsuiting, which provides some fun moments—especially when exploring the open world.

[✔️] 🏁 The large-scale multiplayer races are the game’s most exciting feature. With over 50 players competing at the same time, the chaos of these events can lead to some hilarious and unpredictable moments.

[❌] 🎮 The controls feel inconsistent and frustrating. Biking, in particular, is hard to control precisely, making sharp turns and technical downhill sections more frustrating than fun. The physics also feel floaty and unrealistic, which makes tricks and landings awkward.

[❌] 🔁 The events lack variety and start feeling repetitive after only a few hours. Most races boil down to the same formula: go downhill as fast as possible while avoiding obstacles. There’s little creativity in the course designs, and after a while, everything starts blending together.

[❌] 🏔️ Despite the large open world, exploration feels pointless. Unlike games like Steep, which encouraged you to find unique lines and create your own challenges, Riders Republic lacks meaningful interactions in its world. It ends up feeling more like a giant hub for events rather than an immersive sports playground.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Sound Design & Atmosphere [/h2]

[✔️] 🎧 The soundtrack is filled with energetic rock, hip-hop, and electronic tracks that match the extreme sports theme well. The music does a good job of setting the tone for fast-paced races.

[❌] 🗣️ The dialogue is painfully bad. The game constantly tries to sound "cool" and "edgy," but it comes across as forced and cringeworthy. NPCs throw out cheesy one-liners that get annoying quickly.

[❌] 🎵 The voice lines repeat far too often. Whether it's an NPC hyping you up or a commentator making the same joke for the tenth time, the repetitive dialogue makes the game’s atmosphere feel stale.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Pros and Highlights [/h2]

[✔️] 🌎 The open world is large and packed with different environments, from snowy mountains to dry canyons. While exploration isn't particularly rewarding, the variety of landscapes keeps things visually interesting.

[✔️] 🏆 Multiplayer races are where the game truly shines. The chaotic nature of 50+ player races can lead to some unpredictable and entertaining moments, even if the physics and controls aren’t great.

[✔️] 🚀 The variety of sports is impressive. Being able to switch between biking, snowboarding, skiing, and wingsuiting at any time keeps things from becoming completely stale.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Cons and Drawbacks [/h2]

[❌] 🎮 The controls and physics are frustrating, making the gameplay feel more annoying than rewarding. Landing tricks doesn’t feel satisfying, and movement often feels floaty and unnatural.

[❌] 📜 The game quickly becomes repetitive. Despite the variety of sports, most events feel the same, and there’s little incentive to keep playing beyond the first few hours.

[❌] 🗣️ The dialogue and writing are some of the worst I’ve seen in a game. The forced "cool" and "quirky" style of speech is cringeworthy and ruins immersion.

[❌] 🚴‍♂️ The world feels empty and underutilized. While the map is large, there’s very little to do outside of marked events, making exploration feel pointless.

[hr][/hr]

[h2] Why 5/10? [/h2]
Riders Republic had the potential to be an exciting extreme sports game, but it falls short due to frustrating controls, repetitive gameplay, and an over-the-top attempt at being "cool" that just doesn’t work. While the large multiplayer races provide some fun, the lack of polish and depth makes the overall experience forgettable.

I'm not sure I've ever authored a Steam review of any true substance. I don't intend to write an essay. I am writing this as a dribble of thoughts I've had recently as a vetted PC gamer of 25+ years, and in-particular of MMO, MMORPG, and extreme-sports games. Throughout game reviews I've read, I generally do concur: the game has solid mechanics for having a solid time blasting your way through various American-inspired landscapes, points of interest, parks, and other areas doing every imaginable variant of extreme sport. Yes, it's cool that with the flick of a joystick I can switch from a BS board-slide to a FS crooked. Yes, it would've been prudent to emulate a balance mechanic. See Tony Hawk series...or any skateboarding, or better yet; any BOARD-ing series, period. Besides the obvious disconnect between how cool the physics and tricks look 
 irrespective of the sport and how good they feel yet simultaneously how pathetically vacant the gameplay itself feels...there is the most obvious problem... That is, the game is marketed as, and I quote "Jump into a massive multiplayer playground! Bike, ski, snowboard, or wingsuit across an open world sports paradise."

There is no "massive multiplayer playground". Forming a group, chatting with other users, adding friends, and even light consistent general social communication is scarce to (mostly) non-existent. You don't race against other users; you're allegedly racing ghosts of other users' performances, recorded by Ubi's cloud at some point in time. The skill of these users' ghosts (their performances) increase in difficulty as you increase the gameplay difficulty; which is Ubi actually just cutting budget by working AI in for free by relying on users randomly speeding down their pointless slopes to generate actual competitors... It's EXTREMELY stupid, and isn't multiplayer. It's just competing against a leaderboard with the luxury of visual aid, which actually isn't a luxury; it's blatantly annoying, and the moment you feel immersed you realize you're just speeding down a mountain against nobody. It's almost probably a better idea to turn off (which is an option, as Ubisoft is aware their "multiplayer" game sucks) other players' visibility, because the game is basically a half-baked singleplayer game with the illusion that there will be multiplayer gameplay. Allow me to be very clear; being able to see performances that were once recorded by your game engines cloud does not render a game "multiplayer".

Downgrade compared to Steep

I played quite a bit of Steep and was excited for Rider's Republic since it was announced and was very excited at the potential for another Steep-like game! After its announcement I didn't hear anything about it, but when I found out it was on sale I picked it up for $20, and honestly I don't think I would have paid more for it. I'll talk about it from a Steep fan POV as well as a regular player POV.

In relation to Steep it's an okay Steep successor; it has similar features (like session markers, custom race content, etc) that Steep fans will like and the gameplay is roughly similar to Steep but with new sports and gear to use. There's a noticable absence of the Bone Collector progression and instead seems to focus you more on 'getting good' instead of crashing in fun ways, which is a little disappointing.

However, comparisons to Steep aside I think even for a general audience there's a lot of UX and game design decisions feels either a little sloppy or strangely directionless, and its microtransaction economy is one of the worst I've seen in a Ubisoft title to date.

UX: When dropping into the game it immediately puts you into a race scenario, and you can tell they wanted to get you directly into the action. But after that begins a series of forced introductory cutscenes and missions that took me about 1.5 hours to complete. Some cutscenes I could skip through, while others (like video call or ones that play when you unlock new content on the map) force me to sit through them even when I'm not interested. Generally speaking it feels like the directors couldn't decide if they wanted the player to get in on the action right away or onboard them slowly, and it ends up falling flat on its butt on both fronts.

Gameplay: Some mechanics just feel sloppy or purposeless.

For example there's a 'rewind' mechanic like Forza that lets you rewind your progress at any time to a previous state in the race. The game seems to tout this as a thing you should be using, but I've found it to be very intrustive. Firstly, it resets you facing forward, even if you were turning, which has the possibility of sending you careening in a different direction from your rewinded point. It also doesn't preview your momentum very well, which can make it hard to know if you should be breaking, gliding or accelerating at your restored point. It also doesn't stop the timer during some race types, which makes the prospect of using it instead of just restarting the race pointless if you're on any difficult aside from the easiest one.

There's also swarms of AI riding around the world, and following them can show you where major paths and courses are in the open world. It's a neat technical feature at a glance - some of them just jump around in place or mimic the behaviour of players randomly goofing off. However you'll soon notice that they phase in and out of existence at the start and end of their lines like some kind of Matrix glitch, and if you stand in place you'll see that they're all actually the same characters repeating the exact same action over and over on a short loop. What makes them extremely unbearable is that there's some sources and challenges that require pinpoint precision which become 1000x harder when you have a swarm of 12 AI jumping around and flying this way and that in front of your screen. There's no option to turn them off, they add little, and get old very quickly.

Realization: What was nice about Steep was that generally the 'realization' and justification for the world was pretty minimal. You were just a person on a mountain doing sports and events. For some reason the direction here decided it needed to double-down on rationalizing this premise - like some Ubisoft Executive looked at the premise and complained that it 'didn't make enough sense' or something - and it hurts the game so much.

Now there's a cast of characters who all talk with dialog and "cool" lingo written as though a 45 year old man tried to imagine how a 15 year old talks (bless the writers, I can only imagine finding 100 different ways to write dialog basically just telling you to "Go play [x] event" or "You did a good job" would be such a pain in the butt).

The world itself is also full of branded tie-ins, which I understand is standard for Sports Games but feels out of place here - most Fast Travel points have a Ford F-150 in front of them framed perfectly in camera when you travel to them (which you'll be doing a lot) while CLIF is featured in the main HUB and Prada has a line of in-game events you can complete. It just feels aggressively integrated for even a sports title.

I personally thought the art direction in previews looked cool at the time, but after playing for a while it felt really aimless. The world is a...eco-tech-neon-punk 'rider's paradise' but it's really difficult to nail down what the 'look' its going for even is. Players are given clothing items to either look like a regular joe or a character straight out of Fortnite. It's whiplash inducing and generally a look that feels like Ubisoft Direction generally just didn't have a solid vision for what the game's world should look like at all and it really shows. Maybe some Executive looked at Watch Dogs Legion and said 'idk make it like that I guess'.

World: The mountains, forests, canyons outside of the manmade stuff is pretty, however I find that unless you're travelling on the more level defined paths in the world it's easy to bump into stuff and feel like you're in the wrong place. I found Steep was much more forgiving when it comes to exploration and 'carving out' your own path in the world, but here if you go the wrong way it's much more likely to feel like you're *going the wrong way*

Economy: This is the most painful part to me. I understand games are expensive to make and am typically skeptical when people complain about game pricing, but I do think Rider's Republic is one of the weirder monetization schemes out there.

It's a premium game you pay full price (~$75) for, but its in-game economy is structured like an MMO. Most gear like bikes and skis are earned through events which is nice, but I noticed I played 5 hours and had no new cosmetics and a ton of 'Bucks' to spend. Steep rewarded cosmetics fairly regularly, so I was surprised I hadn't got anything new and decided to check out the in-game shop.

I checked the in-game shop and noticed that I could afford exactly 1 outfit from the shop with my in-game money, but the selection was really limited. There was maybe 16 items in total and out of those 16 maybe 11 of them were premium-currency only. I looked some stuff up online and learned that not only is this normal, the shop also cycles content *weekly*, so if you don't like anything in the shop that week you better be ready to come back next week and try again.

It's an arbitrary restriction that you can tell they lifted from F2P MMO models to enforce user retention and get people coming back with their friends again and again, but I need to reiterate that this is a paid game that costs $80 regularly. I don't think I'd play this on a *weekly* basis, especially not just to see what's in the store, and since I already paid for the game I'm doubtful I'd every buy the premium currency. This cosmetic store would be fine as an optional side-thing for die-hard fans, but as a casual player it's crazy that I now have tons of money in-game, nothing to spend it on and no cosmetics I feel like buying - it seems like a massive failure in the economy's design. I hesitate to call things 'greedy' but it really does feel like it's overstepping goodwill here.

TL;DR It's a fine (maybe a little worse) successor to Steep that has gameplay annoyances which compound into larger issues, hostile economy design and what feels like sloppy direction on what could have been a much cooler idea.

Every ingredient's there for it to be the ultimate extreme sports title, but it's a product rather than an experience.

The controls are obtuse, often I find that movement is unresponsive and it's a coin flip whether my attempt to do a corkscrew passes through to the game or not. The default bindings are uncomfortable for every scheme. I had to play around for half an hour to find a setup that worked for me but the problem is there's way too many assignable actions for a controller to handle comfortably. A big problem is the camera, stationed directly behind the player or to one side, and is only manually accessible with one control scheme. You can adjust the FOV slightly which helps but there's no adjustable zoom. I wiped out more times to objects I couldn't see in my path or around corners, and even lack of information from where I'll be able to land safely after a jump than from my own incompetence. God forbid you use first person.

The events themselves are pretty miserable. I tried 25~ish on expert for a semblance of challenge but I found myself fighting more against the poorly conveyed terrain and horribly restrictive checkpoints than the AI ghosts I was racing against. The "pop 5 balloons" objectives were particularly awful, most requiring carefully manoeuvring dangerous terrain that lead away from checkpoints, which are mandatory lest the game force rewind you and waste a huge amount of time. At that point you might as well restart the event. The first few downhill bike races the game suggests are fun, fluid and persuaded me to continue playing over my Steam refund timer, which I deeply regret. If I had to compliment one thing it would be the BMX segments, which appear to be the only activity designed with player experience in mind. The overall design philosophy leans more on the serotonin from "the one good run" instead of making sure the player has a good time doing anything they want. If you don't take the game seriously it has a nice, casual appeal.
